name: Ukraine
oneLiner: Ukraine's IT industry is built around outsourcing and remote work for Western clients, and it kept service exports going through the war.
intro: The figures on Ukraine's software industry come from the developer community DOU, industry bodies, the central bank and news coverage. Material on feedback and hierarchy is mostly written by outsourcing vendors and recruiters, and these sources often contradict each other. Practice differs a lot between outsourcing and product companies, and between people living in Ukraine and those working from abroad.

design.text: At the ICPC World Finals, Lviv National University placed fourth in 2008 and Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv placed fourth in 2010, both winning gold medals.

design.text: Ukraine's Hofstede uncertainty avoidance (UAI) score is high, at 95. The outsourcing firm N-iX (2019) links this to a preference for detailed plans and background explanations. The article is written from the seller's side.

failure.text: In a July-August 2024 Deloitte and AmCham survey of 139 executives at member companies, 76% said prolonged blackouts affect their operations. At the same time, 88% said they were prepared for outages and 94% had or were developing a business continuity plan.

sources.title: Deloitte Ukraine: Winter resilience strategy survey

failure.text: IT companies are reported to have handled blackouts by opening coworking spaces with generators and Starlink and by subsidizing employees' backup power.

sources.title: IT-Dimension: Ukraine IT Industry During Blackouts

failure.text: Central bank figures reported by AIN.UA show IT service exports peaking at $7.3 billion in 2022 and falling to about $6.4 billion in 2024 (down 4.2% year on year). According to dev.ua, exports recovered slightly to about $6.66 billion in 2025.

failure.text: An article by the outsourcing firm Alcor, citing DOU surveys, says 38% of IT workers feel burned out. Thirty percent of IT specialists serving in the army receive payments from their IT employer.

sources.title: Alcor: IT and Software Outsourcing to Ukraine

feedback.text: The outsourcing firm N-iX (2019) writes that Ukrainian engineers speak their minds on important technical decisions. This is a seller's claim, and no independent study was found.

sources.title: N-iX: An honest look at Ukrainian software developers

feedback.text: The recruiting firm unicrew (2026) writes that unless expectations are made explicit, developers may not push back hard on poor technical decisions.

sources.title: unicrew: How to Hire Developers in Ukraine (2026 Guide)

hierarchy.text: Ukraine scores high on both Hofstede power distance (PDI 92) and uncertainty avoidance (UAI 95). Edge Executive Services (2024) links this to many-layered hierarchies and a large number of rules.

hierarchy.text: The outsourcing firm Jappware claims that Ukrainian IT companies were early to drop rigid hierarchy and formal communication.

communication.text: An Alcor article citing DOU surveys says 66% of IT workers work fully remotely.

sources.title: Alcor: IT and Software Outsourcing to Ukraine

communication.text: N-iX (2019) says formality at first meetings is a sign of respect, and that the one-to-two-hour time difference with Europe makes it easy to overlap working hours. This is a seller's description.

work.text: In DOU surveys, the share of IT workers registered as FOP (sole proprietors) fell from 87% (2022) to 70% (2024), 57% (2025) and 49% (2026). Workers are moving to Diia.City gig contracts and employment contracts.

sources.title: DOU: Портрет айтівця 2026
DOU: Портрет українського айтівця 2025

work.text: Diia.City gig contracts, introduced in 2022, carry 5% personal income tax, a 5% military levy and social contributions of 22% of the minimum wage. As of October 2026 the regime had more than 4,600 resident companies covering about 217,000 specialists.

work.text: In DOU's December 2025 survey (4,522 responses), the median developer take-home pay was $3,450. A study by the law firm Juscutum and the Diia.City Union found that about 20% of IT professionals work from abroad.

oss.text: GitLab is an open source project that Dmitriy Zaporozhets started at his home in Ukraine in 2011. In 2014 he turned it into a company with Sytse Sijbrandij from the Netherlands.

oss.text: Grammarly (a product, not open source) was founded in Kyiv in 2009 by Max Lytvyn, Alex Shevchenko and Dmytro Lider. Its largest engineering hub is still in Kyiv.

variance: Most material on feedback and hierarchy comes from outsourcing vendors and recruiters, and no primary research was found.

Vendor and recruiter articles contradict each other. employsome (2026), unlike unicrew, says developers are comfortable with technical disagreement, and nCube, unlike Jappware, says formal hierarchy is respected.
Hofstede's individualism (IDV) score for Ukraine was revised from 25 in the older edition to 55 today, and older material still uses the old value.
About 20% of IT workers work from abroad, so "Ukrainian developers" includes both residents and emigrants.
At outstaffing companies and small and medium firms, more than 65% of workers were FOP (2025), and both contracts and culture differ from product companies.
Erin Meyer's Culture Map does not place Ukraine.
